'''John D. Lindl''' (born July 27, 1946 in [[Toledo, Ohio]]) is an American [[physicist]] who specializes in [[inertial confinement fusion]] (ICF).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11605014.html|title=Lindl, John|website=history.aip.org|access-date=2020-02-27|archive-date=August 6, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200806014224/https://history.aip.org/phn/11605014.html|url-status=live}}</ref> He is currently the chief scientist of the [[National Ignition Facility]] at the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/who-works-at-nif/honors/dmts-awards|title=LLNL Distinguished Members of Technical Staff|website=lasers.llnl.gov|access-date=2020-02-27|archive-date=February 27, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200227090313/https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/who-works-at-nif/honors/dmts-awards|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and career ==
Lindl obtained a B.S in [[engineering physics]] from [[Cornell University]] in 1968 and a Ph.D. in astrophysics from [[Princeton University]] in 1972.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/people/management/john_lindl.php|title=Management: John Lindl, NIF & Photon Science|date=2010-05-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527160430/https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/people/management/john_lindl.php|access-date=2020-02-27|archive-date=May 27, 2010}}</ref> His Ph.D. thesis advisor was [[John M. Dawson]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/people/people_of_nif/john_lindl.php|title=People: People of NIF, John Lindl, NIF & Photon Science|date=2010-05-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527163120/https://lasers.llnl.gov/about/people/people_of_nif/john_lindl.php|access-date=2020-02-27|archive-date=May 27, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://plasma.princeton.edu/education/graduate-theses|title=Graduate Theses {{!}} Princeton Program in Plasma Physics|website=plasma.princeton.edu|access-date=2020-02-27}}</ref> 

In the same year, Lindl joined the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]] (LLNL), where he worked for [[John Nuckolls]] in the early days of inertial fusion research (e.g. optimal target design for lasers and particle beams, [[Plasma stability|hydrodynamic instabilities]], plasma development in the cavity and cavity design, implosion symmetry). In 1976, he was involved in the design of the first laser fusion experiments with the [[Cyclops laser]]. In 1983, he was deputy program manager for theory and target design in the ICF program of the LLNL. In 1990, he became head of the Nova Laser program to demonstrate the use of a 1 to 2 megajoule laser for inertial fusion. After the ICF research at LLNL became declassified in 1993, Lindl wrote an overview article in [[Physics of Plasmas]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lindl|first1=John D.|last2=Amendt|first2=Peter|last3=Berger|first3=Richard L.|last4=Glendinning|author4-link=S. Gail Glendinning|first4=S. Gail|last5=Glenzer|first5=Siegfried H.|last6=Haan|first6=Steven W.|last7=Kauffman|first7=Robert L.|last8=Landen|first8=Otto L.|last9=Suter|first9=Laurence J.|date=2004|title=The physics basis for ignition using indirect-drive targets on the National Ignition Facility|journal=Physics of Plasmas|language=en|volume=11|issue=2|pages=339–491|doi=10.1063/1.1578638|issn=1070-664X}}</ref> which then led to his book on inertial fusion in 1997. Lindl became the chief scientist at the National Ignition Facility in 2005, whose construction began in 1997 and was inaugurated in 2009 (with the first large-scale laser target experiments).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://lasers.llnl.gov/newsroom/project_status/2009/june.php|title=Newsroom: Project Status, NIF & Photon Science|date=2010-05-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528000229/https://lasers.llnl.gov/newsroom/project_status/2009/june.php|access-date=2020-02-27|archive-date=May 28, 2010}}</ref>

He has also recently been involved in [[magnetic fusion]] research at the LLNL's [[Sustained Spheromak Physics Experiment]] (SSPX).{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

== Honors and awards ==
Lindl is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He has received awards such as the [[American Nuclear Society]]'s [[Edward Teller Award]] in 1993,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ans.org/honors/recipients/va-teller|title=ANS / Honors and Awards / Recipients / Edward Teller Award|website=www.ans.org|access-date=2020-02-29|archive-date=June 5, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605171553/https://ans.org/honors/recipients/va-teller|url-status=live}}</ref> the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] in 1994, and the Fusion Power Associates Leaders Award in 2000.<ref name=":0" />

In 2007, Lindl received the [[James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics]] for "''30 years of continuous plasma physics contributions in [[high energy density physics]] and [[inertial confinement fusion]] research and scientific management"''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?first_nm=John&last_nm=Lindl&year=2007|title=2007 James Clerk Maxwell Prize for Plasma Physics Recipient|last=|first=|date=|website=American Physical Society|language=en|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2020-02-27}}</ref>
